# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, name the folders the change touched** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Leave out test folders, README edits, and above all any file whose diff is comments only.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

# Publish the Claudinite task dashboard to GitHub Pages.
#
# SEEDED ONCE, AT ADOPTION, and this repo's from that moment. `.github/workflows/` is
# the one directory the nightly update cannot push to — the Action's `GITHUB_TOKEN` is
# refused there — so this file arrives with the adopting session and never converges.
# That is why it is a thin shim: everything that can be updated lives in the mount, and
# only what must be frozen is frozen here.
#
# The site holds NO repository data. It is a shell that calls the GitHub API from the
# viewer's own browser with the viewer's own credential, so publishing it discloses
# nothing a viewer could not already read — someone who cannot see a repo sees nothing
# of it here. Do not bake API responses into the build; that property is the reason a
# public Pages site is a safe host for it.
#
# Configure it in `.claudinite-checks.json`, on the `claudinite-dashboard` entry's
# `config` — not here. Every key is optional.

name: Claudinite dashboard

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths:
      # The mount is the page's source, so a converge that moves it republishes.
      - '.claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-dashboard/**'
      - '.claudinite/shared/engine/**'
      - '.claudinite-checks.json'
      - '.github/workflows/claudinite-dashboard-pages.yml'
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write

# Never two deployments at once, and a superseded build is not worth finishing.
concurrency:
  group: claudinite-dashboard-pages
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 24

      - name: Assemble the site
        run: node .claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-dashboard/build-site.mjs

      # The build exits clean with no `_site` when the mount does not yet carry the
      # dashboard — adopted, not yet converged. Uploading nothing would fail the run,
      # and deploying an empty artifact would replace a working site with a 404.
      - name: Is there a site to publish?
        id: built
        run: |
          if [ -f _site/index.html ]; then
            echo "ready=true" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          else
            echo "ready=false" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
            echo "No _site/index.html — skipping the deploy until the mount carries the dashboard."
          fi

      - uses: actions/configure-pages@v5
        if: steps.built.outputs.ready == 'true'

      - uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v3
        if: steps.built.outputs.ready == 'true'
        with:
          path: _site

    outputs:
      ready: ${{ steps.built.outputs.ready }}

  deploy:
    needs: build
    if: needs.build.outputs.ready == 'true'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: github-pages
      url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
    steps:
      - id: deployment
        uses: actions/deploy-pages@v4

name: "Static site: Deploy to GitHub Pages (reusable)"

# Deploys the repo's EXPLICIT publish set to GitHub Pages. Vendored from the
# static-website pack into the repo's own .github/; workflow_call ONLY — it is
# invoked by "Static site: Publish" at the released commit, so what is live is
# always exactly what was tagged. A repo never dispatches it directly.
#
# The artifact is assembled by the assemble-site composite action from
# `publish_root` + `publish_paths` — an additive list, so the agent-tooling dirs
# (.claude/, .claudinite/), dev tooling, notes and anything else unlisted are
# absent by construction rather than by remembering to exclude them. That also
# sidesteps the dangling-symlink trap that breaks a whole-root Pages upload:
# upload-pages-artifact tars with --dereference, and .claude/skills/* are
# symlinks into the gitignored corpus, empty on a runner.
#
# One-time owner setup in the calling repo: Settings → Pages → Source =
# "GitHub Actions". Until that is set, deploy-pages fails; the caller's failure
# reporter opens the tracking issue.
#
# The calling job must grant `permissions: contents: read, pages: write,
# id-token: write`.
on:
  workflow_call:
    inputs:
      ref:
        description: "Commit to deploy (empty = the default checkout)"
        required: false
        type: string
        default: ""

# Least privilege for a Pages deploy: read the repo, write Pages, mint the OIDC
# token deploy-pages exchanges.
permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write

# Never run two Pages deploys at once; let an in-flight deploy finish.
concurrency:
  group: pages
  cancel-in-progress: false

defaults:
  run:
    shell: bash

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
        with:
          ref: ${{ inputs.ref }}

      - id: cfg
        uses: ./.github/actions/read-site-config

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        if: steps.cfg.outputs.build_command != ''
        with:
          node-version: 22

      # Repo variables the config declares, exported into the build's env.
      # `vars` structurally cannot carry a secret, which is the point: this
      # feeds the step that produces the published artifact.
      - name: Export the declared build variables
        if: steps.cfg.outputs.build_vars != ''
        env:
          DECLARED_BUILD_VARS: ${{ steps.cfg.outputs.build_vars }}
          REPO_VARS_JSON: ${{ toJSON(vars) }}
        run: node .github/actions/read-site-config/export-build-vars.mjs

      # A build_command that needs dependencies installs them itself
      # (`npm ci && npm run build`) — see the config's keys.
      - name: Build the site
        if: steps.cfg.outputs.build_command != ''
        run: ${{ steps.cfg.outputs.build_command }}

      - uses: ./.github/actions/assemble-site
        with:
          publish_root: ${{ steps.cfg.outputs.publish_root }}
          publish_paths: ${{ steps.cfg.outputs.publish_paths }}

      - uses: actions/configure-pages@v5

      - uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v3
        with:
          path: _site

  deploy:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: github-pages
      url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
    steps:
      - id: deployment
        uses: actions/deploy-pages@v4

# Tasks — the per-project work mechanism

How a repo's own Claudinite work runs. A repo schedules **itself**, and
every occurrence of every task is an **issue in that repo** — a `[claudinite-work]`
work item whose labels are its state. That is the work-item queue; what follows is
the contract a task is written to, not how the queue works internally.

**A cadence is one way an occurrence is created, not what a task is.** A task is a
unit of the repo's own work with a precondition, a code-work phase and optionally an
agentic-work phase; `frequency` says only how often the queue offers to run it, and
`manual` — no cadence at all — is a first-class value. Work that fires on an event,
on a condition, or on a force is a task in exactly the same sense as work that fires
nightly, and reads the same contract. Anything reachable from the executor belongs
here rather than in a workflow of its own; see the cron rule below for the narrow
case that genuinely cannot be.

Three responsibilities, strictly separated (owner, 2026-08-06):

1. **The tick** — a vendored hourly Action
   (`.github/workflows/claudinite-scheduler.yml`) that is pure label mechanics
   over the issue list: **instantiate** each recurring task's standing item when
   its anchor comes, **ready** blocked items whose wait has passed, **reclaim**
   dead executor claims. It evaluates no precondition and collects no signal.
2. **The executor** — a pull worker over the queue (the tick's post-tick drain,
   and a `labeled`-event run for latency) that picks the next ready item, claims
   it, evaluates **that one task's** precondition, runs its code-work, and either
   converges the item or hands off to an agent session.
3. **The task-janitor** — an ordinary daily task (`basics/task-janitor`,
   `agent_model: none`) that owns everything about the queue that is *nobody's
   task*: items stuck ready past their period, items wearing no state label after
   a torn transition, and a health review of the open set.

The engine is vendored under `.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/`; the basics
pack owns the conformance guards for the surfaces a repo authors around it —
scheduling is baseline Claudinite discipline, present wherever basics is
declared (everywhere), not an opt-in feature.

There is no watermark and no per-run state: an occurrence exists because its
issue exists, which is why an outage self-heals by looking at the queue rather
than by replaying a ledger.

## What the checks guard

- **The scheduler workflow is a thin shim.** The vendored
  `claudinite-scheduler.yml` carries a single **hourly** cron on a repo-hashed
  minute constrained to **:10–:50** (the one repo-specific value in the stub —
  `engine/scheduler/hash-minute.mjs`, a pure function of the repo full name that
  bootstrap stamps in and baselining re-derives), a `concurrency` group, a
  `workflow_dispatch` trigger (whose one `wake` input is how a task is forced,
  here or from another repo), and a call into the vendored tick — no logic of its own
  (schema and behaviour changes ride the vendor refresh, not workflow edits). It
  is the repo's **only** cron; the executor's workflow beside it carries none. Work
  that had its own cron'd workflow becomes a **task**, and that workflow is deleted
  — its steps move into the task's worker. So does work with no cron at all: an
  event-driven or condition-gated job becomes a task on `frequency: 'manual'`, woken
  by whatever knows the event happened. Don't keep either as a dispatch-only workflow
  for the task to fire: that is two files and two edit sites for one job, and a
  workflow whose only caller is the thing that replaced it. (A workflow that must run
  *as an Action* for something a task cannot reach — an Actions-only secret, an OIDC
  identity a deploy target demands — is the exception. Even then the task owns the
  trigger and the decision to run; the workflow carries only the step that needs the
  Action's own privileges.) Off-band or multiple
  crons, or a missing concurrency/dispatch guard, break staggering, double-run
  safety, or manual runs.

- **Every task declaration carries the full contract.** A `tasks/<name>/task.mjs`
  default-exports `id` (matching its directory), `frequency` (`hourly | daily-2h
  | daily-1h | daily | daily+1h | weekly | monthly | manual`), `precondition_signals` (the collector
  vocabulary), `agent_model` (`opus | sonnet | haiku | none`), `expected_outcome` (`none |
  open-pr | merged-pr`), and a `precondition`. An agentic task (`agent_model !==
  none`) also carries `agent_instructions`, the worker file the agent reads; a
  `none` task runs no agent, so the field is not applicable and is omitted. The
  tick and executor read agent_model/expected_outcome/frequency from this file — never from the work
  item — so an illegal or missing value means a task never fires, fires wrong,
  or writes past its declared ceiling. The same contract
  (`engine/scheduler/task-contract.mjs`) is re-validated at run time, so the
  static and runtime views can't drift. A task declares **no session scope** — see
  the next entry.

- **A task's code reads only the environment code-work is handed.** Code-work runs as

# Reusable workflow: builds a repo's privacy policy into a one-page GitHub
# Pages site and deploys it at the fixed permalink /privacy/ —
#   https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/privacy/
# The Jekyll `permalink` pins that public path independent of where PRIVACY.md
# lives in the repo (move the file → only the input below changes, never the
# URL). The page body is the caller's PRIVACY.md verbatim — the single source
# of truth, no duplicated copy.
#
# Deliberately NOT Chrome-specific (hence the unprefixed name): any publish
# standard whose store listing needs a live privacy-policy URL deploys through
# it. workflow_call ONLY — it never runs in Claudinite itself. It is invoked by
# "Chrome extension: Publish to Chrome Web Store" so the page is refreshed
# whenever the listing ships (and, because that publish workflow runs this leg
# even when the upload leg fails, it's also how the /privacy/ URL first goes
# live before the first publication). There is no standalone privacy dispatch
# stub — a repo never calls this directly.
#
# One-time owner setup in the calling repo: Pages source = "GitHub Actions"
# (repo Settings → Pages). Production deploys only from the default branch (the
# github-pages environment's branch policy), so the calling stub must be on
# `main` to publish.

Short answer: because a Pages deploy is one of the few things a Claudinite task structurally *cannot* do — and that exception is already written down in the contract.

**The rule** ([`packs/core/scheduled-tasks.md:47-57`](packs/core/scheduled-tasks.md)) says work with its own cron'd workflow becomes a task and the workflow gets deleted, and so does event-driven or condition-gated work (a `frequency: 'manual'` task, woken by whatever knows the event happened). Then the carve-out, verbatim:

> (A workflow that must run *as an Action* for something a task cannot reach — an Actions-only secret, an OIDC identity a deploy target demands — is the exception. Even then the task owns the trigger and the decision to run; the workflow carries only the step that needs the Action's own privileges.)

**Pages is exactly that OIDC case.** `actions/deploy-pages@v4` doesn't push a branch — it exchanges a GitHub OIDC token (`id-token: write`) for a deployment against the `github-pages` environment, and the artifact has to arrive via `actions/upload-pages-artifact` from the same run. A Claudinite task runs inside the executor's session with the executor's own token and job identity; it can build `_site` perfectly well, but it has no way to mint that identity or hand an artifact to the Pages deployment API. So the deploy leg has to be a job in a workflow, not a step in a task.

Three of the four Pages workflows here already follow the "carry only the privileged step" half of the rule: [`static-site-deploy-pages.yml`](packs/static-website/stubs/workflows/static-site-deploy-pages.yml) and [`deploy-privacy-page.yml`](.github/workflows/deploy-privacy-page.yml) are `workflow_call`-only — they hold no trigger and no decision, and something else decides when to publish. [`claudinite-dashboard-pages.yml`](packs/claudinite-dashboard/stubs/workflows/claudinite-dashboard-pages.yml) is the one that still owns its own `push:` trigger, and its header gives a second, independent reason it's frozen there: `.github/workflows/` is the one directory the nightly converge can't push to, so the file is seeded once at adoption and deliberately kept as a thin shim with everything mutable in the mount.

Worth flagging, since your question points straight at it: the dashboard workflow is the one place where the "the task owns the trigger and the decision" half isn't satisfied — the `paths:` filter on the mount is the decision, and it lives in a file nothing can update. If you want that tightened, the shape the rule asks for is a `frequency: 'manual'` task that decides and builds, woken by the converge, calling a `workflow_call`-only deploy leg. Say the word and I'll open an issue for it.

# the poll that makes a lost label event irrelevant, so events here are latency
# sugar and never the only delivery.
#
# THIS IS THE ONLY PLACE SECRETS LIVE (DESIGN §14). The wiring converge stamps
# every task's declared `required_secrets`, plus each configured invocation
# endpoint's token secret, into the step env below by name — the tick and the
# janitor get none, because they never execute task code. Code-work is the only task
# code that ever sees a value; the agent hop carries nothing.
#
# MORE CAPACITY IS MORE EXECUTORS. Nothing enumerates them and each claim is
# independently leased, so a second job, a matrix width, or a runner outside
# Actions entirely all work — the executor's whole interface is issue read/write
# plus the repo at HEAD.
name: Claudinite executor

on:
  issues:
    types: [labeled]
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: write
  issues: write
  pull-requests: write
  actions: write

jobs:

    # A label event on anything else is not this workflow's business — and a
    # workflow_dispatch carries no label at all, so it always runs.
    if: >-
      github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch'
      || github.event.label.name == 'task:ready'
      || github.event.label.name == 'task:urgent'

    # killed by the platform before its claim is reaped and the item re-picked, or
    # a zombie's code-work runs beside its replacement's (F17).
    timeout-minutes: 50
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - name: Pick up and execute ready work

          CCR_FLEET_ROUTINE_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CCR_FLEET_ROUTINE_TOKEN }}

You're right, and my previous answer overstated it. Code-work does run inside the executor's Action job, so "a task structurally cannot reach an OIDC identity" is wrong. If the executor job declared `pages: write` and `id-token: write`, code-work would get `ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL` and `ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN` in its env like any other step, and `actions/deploy-pages` is only a thin JS action over that — mint an OIDC token for the Pages audience, POST to the deployments API. Nothing about that needs to be a separate workflow.

So the honest reason is not capability. It's these, in descending strength:

**1. The executor is one job for every task.** [`claudinite-executor.yml:24-28`](.github/workflows/claudinite-executor.yml) grants `contents/issues/pull-requests/actions`. There's no per-task permission scoping — adding `id-token: write` there hands *every* task's code-work in *every* member repo the ability to mint OIDC tokens, forever, so one deploy task widens the blast radius of the file whose own header calls it "THIS IS THE ONLY PLACE SECRETS LIVE". That's the real cost, and it's fleet-wide because the workflow is vendored.

**2. Concurrency has no task-level equivalent.** Pages rejects overlapping deployments; today `concurrency: group: pages` handles it at the workflow level. The executor explicitly supports multiple concurrent executors ("MORE CAPACITY IS MORE EXECUTORS… each claim is independently leased"), and the queue has no cross-item mutex. Two deploy items in flight is a state the queue is designed to allow.

**3. We'd own a reimplementation of two first-party actions.** `upload-pages-artifact` tars with `--dereference` and uploads through the runner's artifact API; `deploy-pages` polls the deployment to a terminal state. Rewriting both in vendored engine code means a GitHub-side change breaks every member at once, against a workflow-level `@v3`/`@v4` pin that today just moves.

Note the split that makes your point exact: **code-work** runs in the Action, **agent-work** does not — it hands off to a Claude session with no Actions identity at all. So the capability argument I gave only ever applied to the agentic half.

Given that, the carve-out sentence in [`packs/core/scheduled-tasks.md:53-57`](packs/core/scheduled-tasks.md) is miswritten: it justifies the exception on "an OIDC identity a deploy target demands", which as you've shown isn't a wall. The defensible version is about *scoping* — a privilege that must not be granted to every task in the repo belongs in a job that only the deploy runs. Want me to open an issue to fix that sentence?

> ⚠️ Still open: my prior answer's "structurally cannot" was wrong — corrected above. The carve-out in `scheduled-tasks.md` is justified on the wrong grounds; no edit made, awaiting your call on opening an issue.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, name the folders the change touched** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Leave out test folders, README edits, and above all any file whose diff is comments only.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

# Chrome extension — release & Chrome Web Store publication standard

Every Chrome-extension repo of ours ships the **same** release pipeline: same workflows, same
Chrome Web Store API usage, same secrets, same versioning and artifact rules, same README install
sections. This doc is that contract, the setup steps for a new extension repo, and the manual
Chrome Web Store actions the automation can't do. The workflow **logic** is authored once, in this
pack's [`stubs/`](stubs/) — the [orchestrator](stubs/workflows/chrome-extension-release.yml), the
four `workflow_call`-only **reusable workflows**, and the
[report-failure](stubs/actions/report-failure/action.yml),
[read-release-config](stubs/actions/read-release-config/action.yml) and
[bump-extension-patch](stubs/actions/bump-extension-patch/action.yml) composite actions — and
**vendored into each extension repo's own `.github/`**, where the whole pipeline runs with no
cross-repo dependency. GitHub only resolves a reusable workflow or composite action from a repo's
own `.github/`, so "the logic lives in the pack" means the pack holds the templates and each repo
hosts a *managed* copy: the pack keeps every copy in sync — baselining re-materializes on drift via
the `chrome-release-vendoring` migration — so a repo **hosts** the pipeline without **owning** it.
Treat the vendored `.github/workflows/` + `.github/actions/` set as generated: edit the pack, not
the copy. A repo adds only its **required** `.github/release.config` (five explicit keys, **no
defaults**). A merged canon change reaches every extension repo through the nightly baselining, not
a live `@main` reference. Everything a repo used to carry as workflow values — the version files, the
zip location, the test gate, the shipping set, and the previously per-repo `bump`/`filter` scripts
— is either pack logic (the bump/filter, and `npm run build`) or an explicit `release.config` key,
so no repo ships a bump or filter script any more. Reference implementation:
`missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator`; also adopted by `TLDR` and `CrosswordChat`.

Naming in the flat `.github/workflows/` namespace: Chrome-specific logic carries the
`chrome-extension-` prefix (future publish standards — other stores — will live beside it);
genuinely platform-agnostic pieces (`deploy-privacy-page.yml`, the `report-failure` action) keep
general names so other standards reuse them as-is. When in doubt, prefix.

## The contract

**Versioning**

- The extension manifest's `version` (`X.Y.Z`) is the single source of truth. The extension's
  `package.json` `version` must equal it, enforced by a CI-run guard (a unit test or an inline
  workflow check — the repo picks the mechanism, the invariant is fixed).
- Minor/major bumps are deliberate and human: **"bump version"** = edit the manifest and
  `package.json` (plus any repo version-sync constant) together on a branch — default the next
  **minor** — and land on `main` via a normal PR. Merging the bump *is* cutting the release.
- Patch bumps belong to the daily auto-release. No workflow other than the daily bump ever
  changes the version; "Release: Create Package" never does.

**Artifact**

- `npm run build` produces the zip at the **forced-uniform** standard location
  `dist/<kebab-cased repo name>.zip` (e.g. `dist/google-calendar-event-creator.zip`, `dist/tldr.zip`,
  `dist/crossword-chat.zip`) — the place/name is derived, not a config choice; a repo's build must
  write there. Stable, never version-stamped, so
  `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/releases/latest/download/<zip>` is a permanent
  newest-build URL. `manifest.json` sits at the zip's top level.
- The zip's contents come from a single shipping-set source of truth in `dev/build/release/`,
  drift-guarded by a test — nothing dev/test-only ships, and a renamed runtime file fails the
  build rather than silently dropping out of the package.
- A release is GitHub Release **`vX.Y.Z`**, tagged at the released commit, with auto-generated notes
  and **two** assets built from the one tested tree, differing only in the injected `API_BASE_URL`:
  the headline **`<zip>`** (the permanent `…/releases/latest/download/<zip>` URL) is built with
  `API_BASE_URL` **cleared**, so it keeps the committed **dev** default — the downloadable build is
  dev, never prod; **`<zip>-prod.zip`** carries the injected prod `API_BASE_URL` and is the store's
  source of truth (the publish job downloads it). So **only the store submission is prod-pointed**;

# baked into the reusable workflows, so collapsing to one entry point loses no
# per-operation triage.
#
# secrets: inherit passes the four CHROME_* store secrets through to the reusable
# workflows.
#
# A repo whose build bakes in per-environment config (e.g. an API base URL)
# uncomments a build_env block on the create-package and daily jobs — the ONLY
# place a repo references its repository variables; every key must be non-empty
# or the run fails, so a mis-configured zip can't ship. Example:
#       build_env: |
#         API_BASE_URL=${{ vars.API_BASE_URL }}
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  schedule:
    - cron: "30 0 * * *"
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      mode:
        description: "What to run"
        type: choice
        options: [publish, package, daily]
        default: publish
      tag:
        description: "publish: release tag to publish (blank = latest release)"
        required: false
        type: string
      auto_publish:
        description: "publish: publish to users after upload (uncheck = dashboard draft)"
        type: boolean
        default: true

permissions:
  contents: write
  pages: write
  id-token: write
  issues: write

# Daily runs (scheduled, or a mode=daily dispatch) share one queue so a manual
# dispatch can't race the scheduled bump-push; every other run gets its own group.
concurrency: >-

       (github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' && inputs.mode == 'daily'))

jobs:
  create-package:
    if: >-

      (github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' && inputs.mode == 'package')

    if: github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' && inputs.mode == 'publish'
    uses: ./.github/workflows/chrome-extension-publish-store.yml
    with:
      tag: ${{ inputs.tag }}
      auto_publish: ${{ inputs.auto_publish }}
    secrets: inherit

    if: >-
      github.event_name == 'schedule' ||
      (github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' && inputs.mode == 'daily')
    uses: ./.github/workflows/chrome-extension-daily-release.yml
    secrets: inherit

content.text:
No — and the chrome-extension release is actually the *strongest* case for keeping a workflow layer, not the weakest. But it also shows the split is already drawn where I said it should be.

**It's already a task-owns-the-trigger design.** [`tasks/store-release/task.mjs`](packs/chrome-extension-release/tasks/store-release/task.mjs) is `agent_model: 'none'`, `frequency: 'daily'`, and its worker's only job is to dispatch the orchestrator's daily leg. The pack even enforces the handover: [`release-workflows.mjs:96-106`](packs/chrome-extension-release/release-workflows.mjs) reads whether `claudinite-scheduler.yml` exists in the repo and *flips the requirement* — before cutover the orchestrator must carry the `00:30` cron, after cutover it must have none. (I initially read the `schedule:` still in the stub as drift; it isn't — it's the pre-cutover half of that gate.)

**What's left in workflows is a graded permission ladder, and that's the point.** [`chrome-extension-daily-release.yml`](packs/chrome-extension-release/stubs/workflows/chrome-extension-daily-release.yml) runs five jobs at five different privilege levels: `check` at `contents: read`, `bump` and `release` at `contents: write`, `publish` at `contents: read` + `pages: write` + `id-token: write` + `secrets: inherit`, `report-failure` at `issues: write`. The four `CHROME_*` store secrets touch exactly one of those jobs.

Collapse that into code-work and the executor becomes one job holding the union. And the executor has no per-task secret isolation — its header says the converge stamps *every* task's `required_secrets` into one step env, which is what [`claudinite-executor.yml:44-56`](.github/workflows/claudinite-executor.yml) shows. So the credential that can publish to real Chrome Web Store users would be in the environment of every task's code-work in that repo — `tidy-issues`, `growth-extract`, all of them. That's a much worse trade than the Pages case, where the widened grant was only OIDC.

Three more that are structural rather than about secrets:

- **Multi-job with re-checkout.** `bump` pushes a commit, then `release` is called with `ref` pointing at the *new* commit — the run was triggered before that commit existed. That's `needs:` plus a fresh checkout per job. Code-work is one process in one tree, sharing a 50-minute leash with the rest of the queue.
- **`concurrency` and the audit surface.** The `daily-release` group, the `auto_publish` dispatch toggle, the per-job logs, and `report-failure` filing a tracking issue are all workflow-native. A publish reaches real users irreversibly; that deserves its own run record, not a line in an executor log.
- **The precondition genuinely can't decide.** The task's own comment says so: it's a "cheap pre-filter" because `.github/release.config` isn't in a precondition's scope, so the workflow's `check` job does the authoritative shipped-file diff.

**Where I'd actually push back on the current design:** that last one is the seam worth moving. The decision "is there something to ship" lives in two places — the task precondition and the `check` job — and the reason is a signal-collector limitation, not a law. If a collector could read `release.config` and diff shipped paths, the task would own the whole decision and the workflow would be pure execution, which is what the rule asks for. That's the part that should move, not the publish.

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. content.text:
Sorry — I jumped to asking about filing before actually answering you. Here's the answer.

**No, it shouldn't be 100% tasks — and the chrome-extension release is the strongest case *for* the split, not against it.** It sharpens the same argument rather than changing it.

The reason is the permission ladder. [`chrome-extension-daily-release.yml`](packs/chrome-extension-release/stubs/workflows/chrome-extension-daily-release.yml) runs five jobs at four different privilege levels: `check` at `contents: read`, `bump` and `release` at `contents: write`, `publish` at `contents: read` + `pages: write` + `id-token: write` with `secrets: inherit`, `report-failure` at `issues: write`. The four `CHROME_*` store secrets resolve in exactly one job.

The executor is **one job with one `permissions:` block**. Folding this into a task means every task's code-work in that repo runs at the union of all five — including credentials that can push a build to real users. Note the asymmetry that makes this structural: the executor header says it stamps each task's declared `required_secrets` into the step env, so there *is* a per-task secrets mechanism. There is no per-task *permissions* mechanism. A task can be scoped to its secrets; it cannot be scoped to its GitHub token grants.

Two more that are specific to release rather than to Pages:

- **The 50-minute leash.** [`claude-executor.yml:41-44`](.github/workflows/claudinite-executor.yml) caps at 50m and must stay under the engine's 60m executing leash, or "a zombie's code-work runs beside its replacement's (F17)". The release path is full test gate → build → GitHub Release → store upload. A claim reaped mid-publish is two store submissions.
- **Non-idempotency.** Release and publish are the operations where a retry across an unobservable outcome is worst — which your own rule already names: *"check whether declining to retry removes the uncertainty before building dedup or arbitration machinery."* The queue's model is lease-and-reclaim; that's the wrong model for a store submission.

**What's already right:** `store-release` is the reference implementation of the carve-out's second sentence — *the task owns the trigger and the decision to run; the workflow carries only the privileged step*. The precondition decides in code (manifest version ahead of the latest release, or a substantive commit in the window), and [`worker.mjs`](packs/chrome-extension-release/tasks/store-release/worker.mjs) only dispatches. It also absorbed the workflow's own 00:30 cron — and I checked: the `schedule:` still in the stub isn't drift, it's the pre-cutover shape, with [`release-workflows.mjs:89-105`](packs/chrome-extension-release/release-workflows.mjs) gating on `claudinite-scheduler.yml`'s presence so the de-cron'd form travels with the mount rather than ahead of it.

**The one seam worth tightening:** the ship/no-ship decision is made twice. `task.mjs` says so plainly — the precondition is "the cheap pre-filter; the workflow is the exact gate", because `.github/release.config` isn't in a precondition's scope, so the authoritative shipped-file diff happens in the workflow. Two places decide whether to ship. Closing that moves work *toward* the task (teach a collector to read `release.config`), leaving the workflow as pure execution. That's the direction your instinct is pointing, and it's the right one — it just stops at the privilege boundary rather than crossing it.

> ⚠️ Still open: nothing filed — you dismissed the popup. Two candidates remain unrecorded: the `scheduled-tasks.md` carve-out justified on the wrong grounds (OIDC reachability rather than privilege scoping), and the duplicated ship/no-ship decision in `store-release`.

content.text:
You're right on both, and I've now led with the privilege argument twice and had it not survive. Let me concede precisely and say what's actually left.

**Secrets: parity, you're right.** Tasks declare `required_secrets` and the converge stamps them into the executor's step env by name. That's the same granularity `secrets: inherit` + a per-job boundary gives. No argument there.

**Permissions: weaker than I said, and partly self-defeating.** One correction to your phrasing that cuts *your* way as much as mine — the executor has `contents: write`, `issues: write`, `pull-requests: write`, `actions: write`, but *not* `pages: write` or `id-token: write`. So it's two grants short, not zero. But `actions: write` is the one that matters: the executor can already dispatch the release orchestrator, which runs at the full elevated set. **A compromised or buggy task can already cause a store publish today.** The per-job ladder isn't containing the executor from anything — it's containing the release pipeline's own jobs from each other. That's real defense-in-depth but it's a much smaller claim than the one I made, and you're right that we could build per-task permission scoping if we wanted it and simply haven't.

So what actually survives, honestly ranked:

1. **Execution semantics.** This is the real one. The queue is lease-and-reclaim under a 50-minute cap; a claim reaped mid-publish gives you a zombie running beside its replacement — against a store submission that isn't idempotent and whose outcome you can't observe on retry. Today's design sidesteps this precisely by *dispatching and not awaiting*. Make it 100% task and the whole test→build→release→upload chain runs inside the leash under reclaim semantics. That's not a privilege problem, it's a durable-execution problem, and the queue isn't a durable-execution engine.
2. **The `uses:` surface.** The pipeline leans on `softprops/action-gh-release`, `actions/deploy-pages`, `actions/upload-pages-artifact`, and three composite actions. A task is a node subprocess — it can't `uses:`. Going 100% task means vendoring reimplementations of all of them into engine code, where a GitHub-side change breaks every member at once instead of moving a version pin.
3. Concurrency — the orchestrator's `daily-release` group has no queue-level equivalent. Minor.

That's it. Note that none of those are "a task can't reach the privilege" — which is the shape both of my previous answers took, and the shape `scheduled-tasks.md`'s carve-out is written in. The defensible line is narrower than any of them: **the decision belongs in the task; the execution stays in the workflow when it's long-running, non-idempotent, or built on the Actions composition model.** `store-release` already sits on that line, minus the duplicated ship/no-ship gate.

> ⚠️ Still open: conceded the secrets and permissions arguments — what survives is execution semantics and the `uses:` surface, not privilege. `packs/core/scheduled-tasks.md`'s carve-out is now wrong on both my earlier readings and this one; nothing filed or changed.

Rebased to `origin/main` (`ed2039e`). Layout changed: `chrome-extension-release` merged into [`packs/chrome-extension/`](packs/chrome-extension/) — the task is now [`packs/chrome-extension/tasks/store-release/`](packs/chrome-extension/tasks/store-release/task.mjs), workflows under [`packs/chrome-extension/stubs/workflows/`](packs/chrome-extension/stubs/workflows/). `app-store-release`, `play-store-release`, `firebase-release` are new stubs. Everything I checked still holds.

**1. Execution semantics — few words.**
The queue reclaims dead claims and re-runs the item. A publish killed at the 50-minute cap gets re-picked and submitted to the store twice. Today's task dodges this by dispatching and not awaiting (`code_work_timeout: 120`); running the pipeline inline would not.

**2. `uses:` — you're right, essentially Pages-only.**
I grepped it. Non-Pages third-party actions across all five workflows: exactly one, `softprops/action-gh-release@v2`. And that one's thin — `POST /repos/{o}/{r}/releases` plus asset uploads over a token the worker already holds. Everything else is `actions/checkout` and `actions/setup-node` (a task already has both) or our own composite actions (`read-release-config`, `bump-extension-patch`, `report-failure`) which are already node scripts a task could call directly. The genuinely action-shaped set — `configure-pages`, `jekyll-build-pages`, `upload-pages-artifact`, `deploy-pages` — is all Pages. So that argument collapses into the Pages one too.

**3. The problem.**

   150	`agent_model: none` task's worker is a sibling `.mjs` the executor runs as

   155	remainder for **work code-work could not do**, never for a re-check of whether

   161	by it, and every work item names it as the file its run is about. What an
   162	agentless task's worker does is documented in a **`README.md`** beside it.

   169	### Three optional declarations
   170	
   171	Declare one only when its rule applies.
   172	
   173	- **`after: ['<pack>/<task>']`** — this task yields while a named upstream's item is live

   175	  reads what another task produces; never as a general priority hint. It is not a
   176	  `Blocked-by` edge and must not be described as one.
   177	- **`on_interrupt: 'requeue' | 'needs-human'`** (default `requeue`) — declare `needs-human`

   200	  precondition, as code over signals, its verdict binding via the item's

   204	- **A failing worker may say why it failed.** The executor sees an exit code and

   213	
   214	  The kind is `action`, `decision`, `approval` or `failure`; the last marker in the
   215	  output wins, so a worker sweeping many targets may revise its verdict as it goes.
   216	  No marker — and every worker written before this existed — parks at `failure`,
   217	  which is the lane that means "someone reads the trace".

   230

   232	['<pack>/<task>']`**: its item yields while that upstream's item is live this

   241	the same cycle once the upstream is out of the way.
   242	
   243	## The queue labels are the item's state, and only the queue writes them
   244	
   245	A work item's **state is its labels**, and there is exactly one state label on it
   246	at a time: `task:blocked` (waiting on a `Not-before` or a `Blocked-by`),
   247	`task:ready` (available to pick), `task:executing` (an executor holds the claim),
   248	`task:agent` (a session owns it). Beside them: `task:urgent` (pick before anything

   252	
   253	Two rules follow, and both are about not borrowing the vocabulary:
   254	
   255	- **Never put a queue label on an ordinary issue**, from a task or by hand. The
   256	  tick and the executor read them as state, and a label on an issue that is not a
   257	  `[claudinite-work]` item is either ignored or misread — neither is what the
   258	  person applying it meant.
   259	- **A task that wants its own tracking issue owns that issue's whole lifecycle**,
   260	  in its own vocabulary. `needs-human` is the one word shared with the queue, and
   261	  a task reusing it is on the hook for clearing it: nothing sweeps an issue that
   262	  is not a work item.
   263	
   264	Label writes are always **granular** — add and remove named labels, never write
   265	the label set. A set-write replaces from a stale snapshot and clobbers a
   266	concurrent transition, and with a tick and several executors moving labels at
   267	once that is a correctness rule rather than a style preference.
   268	
   269	## An item's identity is its issue number, and a hand-off carries a nonce
   270	
   271	There is no slot id and no occurrence id beside the issue: **`#<n>` is the
   272	occurrence**. It is what a `claudinite-task-exec` record's bracketed field
   273	carries, and the only thing tying that record back to the work it describes.
   274	
   275	A hand-off is an **API call**, not a label event — the executor invokes the
   276	session directly and stamps a nonce on the item first. So a session proves it is
   277	this item's session in code before acting: the task file exists at HEAD, its pack
   278	is declared, the title names that task, the item carries `task:agent`, and the
   279	newest hand-off comment carries the nonce it was given. A nonce mismatch means
   280	the fire named a hand-off that is not the current one — the item belongs to
   281	someone else, or to an earlier episode — and the session stops without labelling,
   282	closing or running anything.
   283	
   284	## Item lifecycle — every exit is terminal, and nothing keeps updating
   285	
   286	- **Succeeded, nothing pending** → `outcome:done`, one comment, issue closed.
   287	- **Parked for a human** → `needs-human` **plus one sub-label naming what is being

   289	  one visible convergence, then it is a person's to look at. Re-queueing it by hand

   291	  precondition is re-evaluated at that pickup — which is what makes the retry safe

   294	    for a person to merge or close. The only park that is not a fault.
   295	  - `task:needs-human-action` — something outside the code must change before this
   296	    can run: a secret set, a scope granted, a routine rewired, an input supplied.
   297	  - `task:needs-human-decision` — the run stopped mid-flight and the next step is a

   299	    violation acceptable.
   300	  - `task:needs-human-failure` — the run broke. A bug, a contract-forbidden shape, a

   302

input.title: writing-tasks: the workflow carve-out is justified on two grounds that are false
input.body:
`packs/claudinite-growth/skills/writing-tasks/SKILL.md` tells an agent when work may keep a workflow of its own instead of becoming a task:

> (A workflow that must run *as an Action* for something a task cannot reach — an Actions-only secret, an OIDC identity a deploy target demands — is the exception.)

Both named grounds are false.

- **"an Actions-only secret"** — code-work runs Action-side and a task declares `required_secrets`, which the wiring converge stamps into the executor. The same section says so five bullets down: *"a workflow that exists only to hold a secret is redundant — fold its work into the task's code-work."* The doc contradicts itself.
- **"an OIDC identity a deploy target demands"** — `id-token: write` is one line in the executor's own `permissions:` block. Any step in that job then gets `ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL`/`_TOKEN`; `actions/deploy-pages` is a thin wrapper over exactly that.

A third ground that comes up in conversation — a one-shot external effect that must not be re-run — is already handled by `on_interrupt: 'needs-human'`, declared a few sections below, not by escaping to a workflow.

What *is* real: a `uses:` step is resolved by the runner out of workflow YAML, and code-work is itself a step's subprocess, so no task in any language can invoke one. Work built on marketplace or composite actions — a Pages deploy is the standing example — keeps a workflow for those steps.

This matters because the sentence is what an agent reads when deciding where *new* work goes, on grounds that don't exist. `app-store-release`, `play-store-release` and `firebase-release` are all empty stubs that will be built against it.

While in the file, one other stale statement: *"Both guards are relevance-first"* sits after seven bullets, from when the section had two. The relevance-gated pair is `task-declaration-shape` and `task-md-only-when-agentic`.
